        <article class="article" aria-label="Notion Electron case study">
          <section class="article-section" id="clipboard">
            <h2>Where does the copy operation go?</h2>
            <p>
              The page sees a method called <code>clipboard.write</code>. Its
              implementation in the preload is a wrapper. The useful question is
              what that wrapper sends, and which code receives it.
            </p>
            <div class="agent-terminal">
              <div class="terminal-header">
                <span class="terminal-title"
                  ><span class="terminal-dots" aria-hidden="true"
                    ><i></i><i></i><i></i></span
                  >Your coding agent</span
                ><button
                  class="copy-button"
                  type="button"
                  data-copy="notion-prompt"
                  aria-label="Copy Notion analysis prompt"
                >
                  Copy
                </button>
              </div>
              <p class="terminal-prompt">
                <span class="prompt-symbol" aria-hidden="true">›</span
                ><span id="notion-prompt"
                  >Use REA to trace how Notion copies text and HTML to the
                  system clipboard. Show the code at each step.</span
                ><span class="terminal-cursor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
              </p>
            </div>
            <p class="caption">
              An example prompt with Notion's local application package
              available to your coding agent.
            </p>

            <h3 class="small-heading">REA finds where to start reading</h3>
            <p>
              Analyzing the tab preload with REA locates the API exposed to the
              page and the call that sends an IPC request. Both findings come
              with source ranges in the minified bundle:
            </p>
            <figure class="workflow-figure">
              <p class="figure-title">REA findings → two places to open</p>
              <div class="rea-query-pair">
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header"><span>Exposed page API</span></div>
                  <pre><code>api_key: "__electronApi"
api_status: "dynamic"
source: preload.js:1:22764–22828</code></pre>
                </div>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header"><span>Renderer IPC call</span></div>
                  <pre><code>operation: "invoke"
channel_expression: "e"
source: preload.js:1:6486–6522</code></pre>
                </div>
              </div>
              <figcaption>
                Selected fields from a fresh
                <code>analyze_javascript_application</code> result on Notion's
                tab preload, recorded with REA 4.1.0. Positions use the original
                bundle's line and zero-based column.
              </figcaption>
            </figure>
            <p>
              The agent opens those locations, finds the clipboard member in the
              assembled API, and reads <code>invokerInMain</code>. Its call site
              supplies
              <code class="notion-channel">notion:clipboard:write</code>. That
              name gives the agent something precise to look for in the main
              bundle. The four excerpts below show the route it connects.
            </p>

            <h3 class="small-heading">Four short pieces of code</h3>
            <p class="caption">
              Simplified from the packaged JavaScript, with readable variable
              names. Unrelated members are omitted.
            </p>
            <ol class="rea-queries">
              <li>
                <h4>Start at the API exposed to the page</h4>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>tab_browser_view/preload.js · API member</span
                    ><button
                      class="copy-button"
                      type="button"
                      data-copy="notion-preload-source"
                      aria-label="Copy Notion preload excerpt"
                    >
                      Copy
                    </button>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code id="notion-preload-source">const clipboardApi = {
  write: invokerInMain(<span class="notion-channel">"notion:clipboard:write"</span>)
};

// Included in the API exposed through contextBridge:
// window.__electronApi.clipboard</code></pre>
                </div>
                <p>
                  This member supplies the channel name. The implementation of
                  <code>invokerInMain</code> tells us how the request leaves the
                  page's process.
                </p>
              </li>
              <li>
                <h4>Resolve the preload's wrapper</h4>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>tab_browser_view/preload.js · IPC helper</span
                    ><button
                      class="copy-button"
                      type="button"
                      data-copy="notion-invoke-source"
                      aria-label="Copy Notion invoke wrapper excerpt"
                    >
                      Copy
                    </button>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code id="notion-invoke-source">function invokerInMain(channel) {
  return (...args) =&gt; invokeInMainAndReturnResult(channel, ...args);
}

function invokeInMainAndReturnResult(channel, ...args) {
  return ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, ...args);
}</code></pre>
                </div>
                <p>
                  The returned function forwards the arguments through
                  Electron's request-and-response IPC. We can now look for
                  <code class="notion-channel">notion:clipboard:write</code>
                  on the main-process side.
                </p>
              </li>
              <li>
                <h4>Check how the receiver is registered</h4>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>main/index.js · handler helper</span
                    ><button
                      class="copy-button"
                      type="button"
                      data-copy="notion-handler-source"
                      aria-label="Copy Notion handler wrapper excerpt"
                    >
                      Copy
                    </button>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code id="notion-handler-source">const handleRequestFromRenderer = {
  addListener(channel, handler) {
    ipcMain.handle(channel, handler);
  }
};</code></pre>
                </div>
                <p>
                  The main process uses another wrapper. Its
                  <code>addListener</code> method registers an
                  <code>ipcMain.handle</code> receiver for that channel.
                </p>
              </li>
              <li>
                <h4>Find the write and its sender check</h4>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>main/index.js · clipboard receiver</span
                    ><button
                      class="copy-button"
                      type="button"
                      data-copy="notion-write-source"
                      aria-label="Copy Notion clipboard receiver excerpt"
                    >
                      Copy
                    </button>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code id="notion-write-source">handleRequestFromRenderer.addListener(
  <span class="notion-channel">"notion:clipboard:write"</span>,
  (event, data) =&gt;
    isNotionWebContents(event.sender)
      ? clipboard.write(data)
      : undefined
);</code></pre>
                </div>
                <p>
                  This is the destination. After checking the sender, the
                  handler passes the supplied data to Electron's clipboard API.
                  The channel and the two resolved wrappers connect the exposed
                  method to this call.
                </p>
              </li>
            </ol>
          </section>

          <section class="article-section" id="rich-clipboard">
            <h2>How does a copied block keep its structure?</h2>
            <p>
              Notion's web editor sends text and HTML through
              <code>electronApi.clipboard.write</code>. It keeps the block data
              locally and puts an ID in the copied HTML to connect them.
            </p>
            <figure class="workflow-figure">
              <p class="figure-title">HTML links to saved block data</p>
              <div class="notion-clipboard-grid">
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>Sent to the system clipboard</span>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code>text: "Project notes"
html: "&lt;p&gt;Project notes&lt;/p&gt;"
    + "&lt;!-- notionvc: <span class="notion-channel">&lt;copy-id&gt;</span> --&gt;"</code></pre>
                </div>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>Saved locally by Notion</span>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code>id: <span class="notion-channel">&lt;copy-id&gt;</span>
mimeTypes:
  text/_notion-blocks-v3-production
    → structured block data</code></pre>
                </div>
              </div>
              <ol
                class="notion-mini-flow"
                aria-label="Restoring rich clipboard data on paste"
              >
                <li>Read the HTML ID</li>
                <li>Find the same local ID</li>
                <li>Restore Notion block data</li>
              </ol>
              <figcaption>
                Illustrative text and ID. The recorded module test restores the
                block data when IDs match; a stale entry returns only text and
                HTML.
              </figcaption>
            </figure>
            <p>
              On paste, Notion looks for the HTML ID and checks it against the
              saved copy. Matching IDs restore the block data.
            </p>
            <p class="caption">
              Clipboard format recorded from web assets cached on July 13, 2026.
            </p>
          </section>

          <section class="article-section" id="continue">
            <h2>More examples and sources</h2>
            <details class="evidence-details" id="markdown">
              <summary>Another example: Markdown tables</summary>
              <p>
                Notion parses Markdown into block data. This example shows how a
                table becomes header and data rows.
              </p>
              <figure class="workflow-figure">
                <p class="figure-title">
                  A table through Notion's Markdown parser
                </p>
                <div class="notion-table-example">
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header"><span>Markdown input</span></div>
                    <pre><code>| A | B |
| - | - |
| 1 | 2 |</code></pre>
                  </div>
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header">
                      <span>Structured parser output · excerpt</span>
                    </div>
                    <pre><code>table · headerRow: true
  table_row
    cells: ["A"], ["B"]
  table_row
    cells: ["1"], ["2"]</code></pre>
                  </div>
                </div>
                <figcaption>
                  Recorded output from an extracted Markdown parser. The table
                  becomes rows and cells.
                </figcaption>
              </figure>
            </details>
            <details class="evidence-details">
              <summary>Another path: the offline SQLite connection</summary>
              <p>
                Notion's renderer requests <code>getSqliteMeta</code> through
                IPC. The main process creates a message channel and gives one
                port to the renderer and the other to a SQLite utility process.
                Subsequent statement batches and results travel over that port.
              </p>
              <p>
                Following this handoff explains where the database work runs,
                and why tracing only the initial IPC request misses the later
                conversation.
              </p>
            </details>
            <details class="evidence-details">
              <summary>Sources and how to read the excerpts</summary>
              <p>
                The clipboard bridge comes from Notion Desktop 7.6.1's
                <code>app.asar</code>: the tab preload and
                <code>main/index.js</code>. The excerpts expand minified
                variable names and omit unrelated code; the sender-check helper
                is shown with its underlying
                <code>isNotionWebContents</code> call.
              </p>
              <p>
                The virtual clipboard and Markdown examples come from web assets
                cached on July 13, 2026, including modules <code>747001</code>,
                <code>58169</code>, <code>736810</code> and <code>422457</code>.
                Those assets have their own version. Saved probes executed
                extracted modules and small harnesses; their outputs describe
                those probes rather than a captured desktop UI session.
              </p>
              <p>
                The REA result shown here is a focused analysis of the saved tab
                preload, recorded with the published REA 4.1.0 package. It
                locates the API and invoke operation. The clipboard member and
                matching receiver are connected by reading their wrapper
                implementations in the package.
              </p>
              <p>
                The Markdown example uses parser module <code>422457</code>.
                Saved module tests show that both page and chat filters preserve
                this table. The paste/import, structured Markdown and AI/chat
                parsers have separate entry points and intermediate formats.
              </p>
            </details>

        <h1>Reconstructing TH04's<br />bullet patterns.</h1>
        <p class="lede">
          A ring of bullets starts with a short angle calculation. Use REA to
          inspect the original DOS function, then follow its instructions into
          readable C++.
        </p>
        <p class="page-meta">PC-98 · 16-bit DOS · C++ and assembly</p>
        <a class="text-link" href="https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04"
          >View the TH04 reconstruction</a
        >
      </div>

              >The PC-98 executable and its bullet-angle helper.</span
            >
          </li>
          <li>
            <span class="flow-label">02 · Inspect with REA</span
            ><strong class="flow-node">Instructions + references</strong
            ><span class="flow-note"

              the executable.</span
            >
          </li>
          <li>
            <span class="flow-label">03 · Read the C++</span

        <article class="article" aria-label="TH04 bullet-pattern case study">
          <section class="article-section" id="ring">
            <h2>How a ring aims at the player</h2>
            <p>
              Elly's attack requests an aimed ring with an initial count of 16.
              One helper calculates the direction of each bullet. The same ring
              can face a fixed direction or turn toward the player.
            </p>
            <div class="agent-terminal">
              <div class="terminal-header">
                <span class="terminal-title"
                  ><span class="terminal-dots" aria-hidden="true"
                    ><i></i><i></i><i></i></span
                  >Your coding agent</span
                >
                <button
                  class="copy-button"
                  type="button"
                  data-copy="th04-prompt"
                  aria-label="Copy TH04 example prompt"
                >
                  Copy
                </button>
              </div>
              <p class="terminal-prompt">
                <span class="prompt-symbol" aria-hidden="true">›</span
                ><span id="th04-prompt"
                  >Use REA to find how TH04 creates a ring of bullets and aims
                  it at the player. Explain the calculation and show the
                  code.</span
                ><span class="terminal-cursor" aria-hidden="true"></span>
              </p>
            </div>
            <p class="caption">
              An example prompt, with the original executable and reconstruction
              checkout available locally.
            </p>
            <p>
              TH04 stores a full clockwise turn in 256 angle units. For 16
              bullets, each index adds 16 units: <code>0, 16, 32, …, 240</code>.
              Adding the player's direction rotates those positions together.
            </p>
            <figure class="explanatory-figure th04-ring-figure">
              <div
                class="figure-viewport"
                tabindex="0"
                role="region"
                aria-label="TH04 fixed and aimed bullet rings; scroll horizontally on smaller screens"
              >
                <img
                  src="../../assets/figures/th04-bullet-ring.svg"
                  width="1000"
                  height="520"
                  alt="Two diagrams of a 16-bullet ring. The fixed ring starts at angle zero. Adding a player direction of 40 rotates every direction by the same amount; the highlighted first bullet points toward the player. Both keep a spacing of 16 angle units, or 22.5 degrees."
                  decoding="async"
                />
              </div>
              <figcaption>
                An illustration of the recovered angle math for count 16, player
                direction 40 and template rotation 0.
                <a href="../../assets/figures/th04-bullet-ring.svg"
                  >Open figure</a
                >
              </figcaption>
            </figure>
            <h3 class="small-heading">
              The firing template in the recovered source
            </h3>
            <div class="code-block">
              <div class="code-header">
                <span>Elly's ring attack · source excerpt</span
                ><button
                  class="copy-button"
                  type="button"
                  data-copy="th04-template"
                  aria-label="Copy TH04 firing template"
                >
                  Copy
                </button>
              </div>
              <pre><code id="th04-template">bullet_template.angle = 0;
bullet_template.group = BG_RING_AIMED;
bullet_template.count = 16;
bullet_template_tune();</code></pre>
            </div>
            <p class="caption">
              These lines select the pattern before difficulty and performance
              tuning.
              <a
                href="https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/blob/0d72e9801a5c14c10384efcbb6734ceccb74ee63/src/main/boss/elly_phase_ring16.cpp#L26"
                >Read the attack's source</a
              >.
            </p>
          </section>

          <section class="article-section" id="rea">
            <h2>What REA returns</h2>
            <p>
              We inspect <code>bullet_velocity_and_angle_set()</code>, the
              function that sets each bullet's velocity and angle. REA returns
              its instructions, pseudocode and references. Three parts of that
              result explain the pattern.
            </p>
            <ol class="rea-queries">
              <li>
                <h4>Check the DOS image before reading its code</h4>
                <div class="rea-query-pair">
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header"><span>Agent → REA</span></div>
                    <pre><code>open_binary
{"path": "MAIN.EXE"}

inspect_native_load_image
{}</code></pre>
                  </div>
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header">
                      <span>REA → agent · selected fields</span>
                    </div>
                    <pre><code>status: "verified"
format: "dos-mz"
load_segment: 4096
header_bytes: 6144
module_bytes: 150114</code></pre>
                  </div>
                </div>
                <p>
                  The check ties the loaded code and relocation records to the
                  supplied executable. The path above is shortened for display.
                </p>
              </li>
              <li>
                <h4>Read the ring's multiply and divide</h4>
                <div class="rea-query-pair">
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header">
                      <span>Agent → REA · <code>analyze_function</code></span>
                    </div>
                    <pre><code>{"procedure": "0x2cfc8"}</code></pre>
                  </div>
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header">
                      <span>REA → agent · instruction excerpt</span>
                    </div>
                    <pre><code>0x2d0eb: MOV AX, SI
0x2d0ed: SHL AX, 0x8
0x2d0f0: MOV DL, byte ptr [0x53af]
0x2d0f9: IDIV BX</code></pre>
                  </div>
                </div>
                <p>
                  <code>SI</code> holds the bullet index. The shift multiplies
                  it by 256, then the division uses the count read from
                  <code>DS:53AF</code>. The maintained source names that field
                  <code>bullet_template.count</code>. The complete sequence
                  appears below.
                </p>
              </li>
              <li>
                <h4>Find where the pattern turns toward the player</h4>
                <div class="rea-query-pair">
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header">
                      <span>Same function result · aim excerpt</span>
                    </div>
                    <pre><code>0x2d190: SUB AX, word ptr [0x53a6]
0x2d198: SUB AX, word ptr [0x53a4]
0x2d19d: CALLF 0x1000:1da8
0x2d1a2: ADD word ptr [BP + -0x2], AX</code></pre>
                  </div>
                  <div class="code-block">
                    <div class="code-header">
                      <span>Corresponding maintained C++</span>
                    </div>
                    <pre><code>group_angle_offset += iatan2(
  player_pos.cur.y - bullet_template.origin.y,
  player_pos.cur.x - bullet_template.origin.x
);</code></pre>
                  </div>
                </div>
                <p>
                  The instruction operands expose two coordinate differences and
                  a direction helper. Its return value is added to the relative
                  ring angle. Source names make those addresses readable; REA
                  lets the agent check the original operations behind them.
                </p>
              </li>
            </ol>
          </section>

          <section class="article-section" id="source">
            <h2>From assembly to readable C++</h2>
            <p>
              Select a step to match the original instructions with the angle
              calculation. This summary follows the aimed-ring path; the full
              source also handles spreads, stacks and random patterns.
            </p>
            <div class="step-comparison" data-step-comparison>
              <div
                class="step-selector"
                role="group"
                aria-label="Follow the TH04 aimed-ring calculation"
              >
                <button
                  type="button"
                  data-select-step="1"
                  aria-pressed="true"
                  aria-controls="ring-assembly ring-source ring-step-detail"
                >
                  <span>01</span> Index
                </button>
                <button
                  type="button"
                  data-select-step="2"
                  aria-pressed="false"
                  aria-controls="ring-assembly ring-source ring-step-detail"
                >
                  <span>02</span> Space
                </button>
                <button
                  type="button"
                  data-select-step="3"
                  aria-pressed="false"
                  aria-controls="ring-assembly ring-source ring-step-detail"
                >
                  <span>03</span> Aim
                </button>
                <button
                  type="button"
                  data-select-step="4"
                  aria-pressed="false"
                  aria-controls="ring-assembly ring-source ring-step-detail"
                >
                  <span>04</span> Rotate
                </button>
                <button
                  type="button"
                  data-select-step="5"
                  aria-pressed="false"
                  aria-controls="ring-assembly ring-source ring-step-detail"
                >
                  <span>05</span> Store
                </button>
              </div>
              <div class="code-comparison">
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>REA · original 16-bit instructions</span
                    ><button
                      class="copy-button"
                      type="button"
                      data-copy="ring-assembly"
                      aria-label="Copy TH04 assembly excerpt"
                    >
                      Copy
                    </button>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code id="ring-assembly"><span class="code-step is-active" data-step="1">0x2cfcf: MOV SI, word ptr [BP + 0x4]
0x2d0eb: MOV AX, SI</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="2">0x2d0ed: SHL AX, 0x8
0x2d0f0: MOV DL, byte ptr [0x53af]
0x2d0f4: MOV DH, 0x0
0x2d0f6: PUSH DX
0x2d0f7: CWD
0x2d0f8: POP BX
0x2d0f9: IDIV BX
0x2d0fb: MOV word ptr [BP + -0x2], AX</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="3">0x2d18d: MOV AX, [0x4650]
0x2d190: SUB AX, word ptr [0x53a6]
0x2d194: PUSH AX
0x2d195: MOV AX, [0x464e]
0x2d198: SUB AX, word ptr [0x53a4]
0x2d19c: PUSH AX
0x2d19d: CALLF 0x1000:1da8
0x2d1a2: ADD word ptr [BP + -0x2], AX</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="4">0x2d1b9: MOV AL, byte ptr [BP + -0x2]
0x2d1bc: ADD AL, byte ptr [0x53ad]</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="5">0x2d1c0: MOV [0xbcc8], AL</span></code></pre>
                </div>
                <div class="code-block">
                  <div class="code-header">
                    <span>Readable C++ · aimed-ring summary</span
                    ><button
                      class="copy-button"
                      type="button"
                      data-copy="ring-source"
                      aria-label="Copy readable aimed-ring calculation"
                    >
                      Copy
                    </button>
                  </div>
                  <pre><code id="ring-source">unsigned char aimed_ring_angle(
    <span class="is-active" data-step="1">int index</span>, int count,
    int player_direction,
    unsigned char rotation)
{
<span class="code-step is-active" data-step="1">    int angle = index;</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="2">    angle = (angle * 256) / count;</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="3">    angle += player_direction;</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="4">    angle += rotation;</span>
<span class="code-step" data-step="5">    return (unsigned char)angle;</span>
}</code></pre>
                </div>
              </div>
              <div
                class="step-detail"
                id="ring-step-detail"
                aria-live="polite"
                aria-atomic="true"
              >
                <p data-step-note="1">
                  <strong>01 · Read the bullet index.</strong> The stack
                  argument is loaded into <code>SI</code>. In a 16-bullet ring,
                  this member index runs from 0 through 15.
                </p>
                <p data-step-note="2" hidden>
                  <strong>02 · Space the directions around a full turn.</strong>
                  <code>SHL AX,8</code> multiplies by 256. The count is
                  zero-extended into a word, then <code>IDIV</code> divides the
                  product by that count. For count 16, each index advances 16
                  angle units.
                </p>
                <p data-step-note="3" hidden>
                  <strong>03 · Add the player direction.</strong> The two
                  subtractions form player-minus-origin coordinates. The
                  direction helper returns an angle in <code>AX</code>; adding
                  it turns the whole ring toward the player.
                </p>
                <p data-step-note="4" hidden>
                  <strong>04 · Add the pattern's rotation.</strong>
                  <code>ADD AL,[0x53ad]</code> adds the template angle. Elly's
                  initial template sets it to zero; other patterns can use the
                  same helper with a rotation.
                </p>
                <p data-step-note="5" hidden>
                  <strong>05 · Keep the final angle in one byte.</strong> The
                  store writes <code>AL</code> to the spawn-angle field. Values
                  wrap after 255, just as the unsigned-byte cast does. The
                  surrounding source also converts this angle and speed into
                  velocity.
                </p>
              </div>
            </div>
            <p class="caption">
              The assembly selects the aimed-ring branch, aim calculation and
              final store. The C++ above is a readable summary. Compiler checks
              below apply to the maintained source in the linked project.
            </p>
            <details class="evidence-details">
              <summary>Read the maintained ring and aim source</summary>
              <div class="code-block">
                <div class="code-header">
                  <span>Ring macro · TH04 branch, excerpt</span>
                </div>
                <pre><code>angle_offset = (i * BULLET_ANGLE_FULL_TURN) / count;
if (i &gt;= (count - 1)) {
    group_complete = true;
}
goto aim_or_no_aim;</code></pre>
              </div>
              <div class="code-block">
                <div class="code-header">
                  <span>Angle and velocity · source excerpt</span>
                </div>
                <pre><code>aim:
    group_angle_offset += iatan2(
        (player_pos.cur.y - bullet_template.origin.y),
        (player_pos.cur.x - bullet_template.origin.x)
    );

no_aim:
    vector2_near(
        bullet_template.velocity,
        (group_angle_offset + bullet_template.angle),
        speed
    );
    bullet_spawn_angle = (group_angle_offset + bullet_template.angle);</code></pre>
              </div>
              <p class="caption">
                <a
                  href="https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/blob/0d72e9801a5c14c10384efcbb6734ceccb74ee63/src/main/bullet/add_impl.hpp#L4"
                  >Ring macro</a
                >
                ·
                <a
                  href="https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/blob/0d72e9801a5c14c10384efcbb6734ceccb74ee63/src/main/bullet/add.cpp#L422"
                  >Aim and velocity source</a
                >
                ·
                <a
                  href="https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/blob/0d72e9801a5c14c10384efcbb6734ceccb74ee63/src/main/bullet/types.hpp#L6"
                  >Angle representation</a
                >
              </p>
            </details>
          </section>

          <section class="article-section" id="checking">
            <h2>Checking the maintained source</h2>
            <p>
              The TH04 project's recorded checks compile the bullet-generation
              code, including this helper, with its pinned Turbo C++ 4.0J
              toolchain.
            </p>
            <div class="verification">
              <div>
                <h3>2,139 matching bytes</h3>
                <p>
                  The compiled bullet-generation code matches a 2,139-byte
                  section of the original executable.
                </p>
              </div>
              <div>
                <h3>Two clean builds</h3>
                <p>
                  Two separate builds produce the same matching bytes. The
                  recorded input hashes match the maintained source shown here.
                </p>
              </div>
            </div>
            <p class="caption">
              Recorded on 3 October 2026.
              <a
                href="https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04/blob/0d72e9801a5c14c10384efcbb6734ceccb74ee63/docs/reconstruction/product/TH04_SEMANTIC_BULLET_GENERATION_V1236.md#validation"
                >Read the compiler checks</a
              >.
            </p>
            <details class="evidence-details">
              <summary>Target identity and analysis scope</summary>
              <div class="evidence-table-wrap">
                <table class="evidence-table">
                  <tbody>
                    <tr>
                      <th scope="row">Original target</th>
                      <td><code>MAIN.EXE</code>, 156,258 bytes, DOS MZ</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                      <th scope="row">Helper entry</th>
                      <td><code>0x2cfc8</code> in REA's loaded image</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                      <th scope="row">Original file offset</th>
                      <td>
                        <code>0x1e7c8</code>, returned by
                        <code>address_to_file_offset</code>
                      </td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                      <th scope="row">Recorded code inspection</th>
                      <td>REA 4.1.0 · 7 October 2026</td>
                    </tr>
                  </tbody>
                </table>
              </div>
              <p>
                Compiler checks cover the complete bullet-add code section,
                including this helper. They also compare its MAP contribution
                and overlapping relocation.
              </p>

                reported ranges.

`website/style-guide.md`:

```md
# REA website writing and design guide

> A good website is like a good paper: easy to follow, clear and concise, with a clean, refined presentation.
>
> — N0zoM1z0

For REA, that means a concrete question, a figure that explains the process,
evidence the reader can inspect, and a useful next step. A clean, refined
appearance comes from precise wording, readable figures, consistent typography
and deliberate spacing.

Use this guide for new pages and revisions. Start from an existing page and
reuse `public/assets/styles.css` and `public/assets/main.js`. Local preview and
publication commands are in [README.md](README.md).

## What a reader should understand

A reader scanning for five seconds should see the subject and the result. After
ten seconds, the main figure should explain the sequence. After fifteen seconds,
the prompt or first example should show how to start.

These are reading goals, not a requirement to fit every investigation above the
fold. Keep the main path short and let readers open the supporting details.

## Write the task directly

Name the software, behavior or action in headings. Give the opening paragraph
one job: explain what the page covers. Use concrete verbs such as install, trace,
read, compare and calculate.

| General wording                                  | More useful wording                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Start with a question.                           | Set up REA.                                                        |
| Follow a feature across the app.                 | Trace an Electron CSV export.                                      |
| Following a copy through Notion.                 | How Notion copies text and HTML.                                   |
| A position becomes a sound.                      | Calculate left/right sound panning.                                |
| Follow the investigation.                        | REA case studies.                                                  |
| Reviewed boundary / source owner / target extent | The helper / its surrounding code / the code section being checked |

Questions also work when they name a behavior: “Where is the CSV created?” and
“How does a copied block keep its structure?” give the reader something specific
to look for.

Explain necessary terms where they first matter. An IPC channel can be described
as a named message between Electron processes. Keep exact API names, addresses
and JSON paths in the code or result they identify.

Give each paragraph new information. A diagram can summarize a sequence, while
the code below explains individual steps. Repeating that REA supplies
instructions, callers and constants in several surrounding paragraphs adds no
new step. Explain that role once, then show the results.

Use captions for useful context: which values are illustrative, where an excerpt
comes from, or what a check covers. Scope a claim positively and precisely:
“The compiled function matches 63 bytes” is more useful than a broad claim
followed by several qualifications.

Search titles and sharing previews follow this standard too. Name the software
or task so someone can understand the page before opening it. Keep titles and
descriptions accurate and concise; use technical terms when they identify the
actual topic. Preserve a clear visible headline rather than repeating search
terms throughout the page. See [README.md](README.md#search-and-sharing-metadata)
for canonical URLs, automatic sitemap generation and sharing assets.

## Build a page around one question

### Introductions and first exercises

Explain reverse engineering with a familiar behavior. Pair a short, authentic
code excerpt with readable logic and a figure that explains the result without
requiring the reader to understand either language. Show a simple agent prompt
and the specific facts REA supplies to answer it.

Put compact setup at the beginning of the homepage: a copyable installation
prompt and the ordinary setup command. Then explain what reverse engineering
means and what it lets someone do, before the worked examples.
Begin each example with its goal and the reason to inspect that program.
Name the actual evidence REA returned and what the agent did with it.
Give long pages a short table of contents with concrete section names. Preserve
the reading width: the homepage uses the side gutter when it has room,
and a collapsible sticky menu on smaller screens. Highlight the current
section, keep fragment links usable without JavaScript, and leave room above
the destination for the sticky control. Offer experienced readers a direct
route from setup to the analysis guides. Keep full case-study previews on the
Showcases page, linked from the opening actions.
Use short labels, selective bold text and the shared blue highlight to make
those facts visible when scanning. Keep source, interpretation and new code
attributed to their respective roles. On mobile, the demo can precede its
supporting code once its purpose is clear.
Show how the reader's task changes using the same question on both sides of a
manual/agent comparison. Let returned evidence make REA's contribution visible.
When showing manual analysis, use authentic instructions and specific analyst
questions: what a command ID means, which call performs arithmetic, or which
operand enters a calculation. Numbered selections can connect the code to
illustrative thought bubbles. Keep the agent side brief: one visible prompt,
a concrete answer, and the evidence used to reach it.

When a small reconstruction makes the finding tangible, let readers change an
input or setting and try the result. Connect inspection, recovered logic,
reconstruction and the new experiment. Keep the recovered rule distinct from
new teaching mechanics, and check it against the inspected program.

Offer a supplied target for the next step. A first exercise should take the reader through
setup, a question, an answer with source references, one prediction they can
check, and a follow-up. Introduce specialized prerequisites when the chosen
target requires them.

### Guides

1. Name the task and introduce a small example.
2. Show a short flow of the relevant files, calls or observations.
3. Provide a copyable agent prompt and its prerequisites.
4. Explain the important code or returned fields.
5. Let the reader try the example, with a command or one ZIP download.
6. State the expected result and where to find it.
7. Offer a specific follow-up question or another relevant guide.

A command should work after the steps immediately before it. Use `npx` for a
first CLI query when global installation is optional. Browser examples should
open the hosted fixture by default; a local URL needs a server-start step. Keep
target paths, debugging endpoints and other required inputs explicit.

### Case studies

1. Introduce the project and the particular feature being examined.
2. Show a figure that explains the investigation or behavior.
3. Give a short example prompt.
4. Pair important REA queries with selected returned evidence.
5. Connect that evidence to readable source or an explanation.
6. Explain how the result was checked.
7. Link the reconstruction repository and supporting sources.

Show REA's useful contribution through a concrete finding: a missing stack
argument, a caller, bytes behind a constant, or source ranges in a packaged
bundle. Explain what the agent does with that finding. Credit source
interpretation, reconstruction and external checks to the work that performed
them.

Keep a second investigation optional. Notion's clipboard path is the main
story; Markdown tables and SQLite are additional examples. Native `<details>`
keeps them available without interrupting the first question.

Keep the explanation on the website. Repository links provide source,
reproduction instructions and further evidence. Use specific links for those
purposes, and immutable commit links for checkpoint-dependent facts.

## Make figures explain a relationship

Each figure should answer a question that a reader can name. Choose the visual
form that fits it:

| Relationship                              | Existing example                         | Useful form                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Analysis and verification steps           | DX-Ball sound pan                        | Flow with separate verification branches                         |
| Code across process boundaries            | Electron CSV export and Notion clipboard | HTML flow with APIs and channel names                            |
| A mathematical transformation             | TH04's fixed and aimed rings             | SVG drawn from the angle formula                                 |
| Original instructions and readable source | DX-Ball and TH04                         | Selectable HTML code with matching step highlights               |
| A request caused by an action             | Notes browser export                     | Flow, observed result table and script excerpt                   |
| Recovered behavior and a new experiment   | Dinosaur speed reconstruction            | Inspected code, playable demo and original-result check          |
| Time blocks and changing output           | Aegis login-code reconstruction          | Adjustable clock, block number and code beside recovered methods |

Use SVG or semantic HTML for diagrams with exact text, numbers and arrows.
Generated illustrations can help explore a layout, but the published labels,
relationships and values need to be checked. [figures.md](figures.md) records the
existing assets and original layout references.

Keep labels short, align related nodes, and give arrows an explicit direction.
Use color to identify the relevant operation or connection. Add a legend when
the visual encoding needs one. Avoid making the diagram repeat the entire page.

State illustrative inputs in the caption. TH04's diagram uses a count of 16 and
a player direction of 40; its dots are calculated from those values. Give an
image useful alternative text, and keep source code as selectable HTML.

On small screens, HTML flows stack. A wide SVG can have its own horizontal scroll
and an “Open figure” link. A diagram should remain readable at its intended
display size; scaling small labels down is not a mobile layout.

## Use the existing visual system

The shared stylesheet defines the site. Its core colors are:

| Token      | Value     | Use                              |
| ---------- | --------- | -------------------------------- |
| `--page`   | `#ffffff` | Page background                  |
| `--ink`    | `#20252b` | Main text                        |
| `--muted`  | `#5b6570` | Secondary text                   |
| `--line`   | `#e0e5e9` | Section and component boundaries |
| `--soft`   | `#f4f6f8` | Code and supporting surfaces     |
| `--accent` | `#294f82` | Links and meaningful highlights  |

Use the system sans-serif stack for prose and the shared monospace stack for
code. The current container is at most 1080px wide, with article text limited to
760px. Reuse the existing heading sizes, line heights, section spacing and
component classes.

Whitespace separates ideas. Thin rules identify sections. Headings establish
hierarchy. The blue accent identifies something useful. Keep these elements
consistent rather than adding a new treatment for each page. Decorative
gradients, large shadows and scroll effects do not help explain the examples.

Agent terminals contain short, copyable prompts. Use the existing continuous
cursor animation and reduced-motion behavior. Label an example prompt as an
example; a real recorded result belongs in an evidence block. Copy buttons
should copy only the intended text, without the prompt symbol or cursor.

Include the shared `↑ Top` link on reading pages, with `id="top"` on the body.
Keep its 44px minimum touch height, safe-area spacing and keyboard focus return.
Use the shared script for visibility and reduced-motion behavior.

Use `minmax(0, 1fr)` for grid tracks that contain long commands or nested panels.
Allow code blocks to scroll within their own area. Check expanded details as
well as the default page. Document-level horizontal scrolling usually means a
component needs a width constraint; hiding it can conceal content.

## Keep evidence accurate and public

Preserve target identity, source locations, relevant versions and the scope of
checks. Keep observations, interpretation and unknowns distinguishable in plain
language. Put lengthy provenance in an evidence document or collapsed details.

Label simplified source and selected instruction excerpts. When compiler checks
apply to the maintained project source, say so; a readable summary is a separate
presentation of the calculation. Historical checks and a fresh REA inspection
retain their own dates and attribution.

Use generic example data and display paths. Machine paths, personal account
identifiers, credentials, local configuration, full vendor bundles and raw
captures belong outside the public website. If a path is shortened in a displayed
query, identify that in its caption and keep the original capture separately.

## Review and publish

Before merging a change:

- Read the default page in order. Check that every section advances the task.
- Open details and confirm that sources and extra examples remain usable.
- Verify commands, prerequisites, expected results and downloadable files.
- Keep links and asset paths working at both `/` and `/rea/`.
- Check desktop, intermediate and mobile widths, including 320px.
- Check copying, downloads, code-step selection, keyboard access and reduced
  motion. Core content and native details should work without JavaScript.
- Confirm that figures and code excerpts agree with the supporting evidence.
- Run site preparation, verification and formatting checks.

Match verification to the change. Copy edits need page and interaction checks.
New analysis or behavior claims need the real evidence that supports them; a mock
or a page-loading check cannot establish those claims.

Follow the PR review and CI process, then publish using the existing manual
`website-pages.yml` workflow on `main`. Its default `both` target publishes the
same verified artifact to Cloudflare and GitHub Pages and checks both published
commit markers. Use `pages` only for an explicitly requested publication while
Cloudflare credentials are being configured.
Ordinary commits should not publish the site. After deployment, check both live
pages and confirm they match the reviewed version. The legacy VitePress build
remains separate from the Pages publisher.

```

`website/wrangler.toml`:

```toml
# Serve only the public website. The default deployment is a workers.dev preview.
name = "rea-website-preview"
compatibility_date = "2026-10-08"
workers_dev = true
preview_urls = false

[assets]
directory = "./public"
html_handling = "auto-trailing-slash"
not_found_handling = "none"

[build]
cwd = ".."
command = "python3 scripts/prepare-website.py && python3 scripts/verify-website.py"
watch_dir = "./public/examples/notes-electron"

# Public HTTPS depends on zone activation and certificate readiness.
[env.production]
name = "rea-website"
workers_dev = true
preview_urls = false
routes = [{ pattern = "rea.tools", custom_domain = true }]

# Production receives the already prepared and verified shared Pages artifact.
# Override the preview build so deployment does not regenerate local assets.
[env.production.build]
command = ""

```
